processing_time.value: Through TAD the average resolution time is 30 working days and the payment takes at least 72 working hours to be confirmed; through a Notarial College the time must be asked of each college

how_to_steps.text: Check that you are over 18 and have a tax key (Clave Fiscal) of level 2 or higher with an Argentine bank account linked to it.
Sign in to the TAD platform, search for Apostilla and start the application for electronic public documents.
Check your details, accept the terms, which say fees are not refunded if the request cannot be processed, and attach the digitally signed document.
Confirm the request and pay the electronic payment slip (VEP) through the Link or Pago mis Cuentas network.
After at least 72 working hours a TAD file number is created, and the apostille, whose number starts with CE, is notified within about 30 working days.
Alternatively, apply in person at the Notarial College of your province, or at an Argentine consulate if you are abroad.

special_rules.text: The procedure is not personal, so anyone over 18 can start it even if they are not the holder of the document.

Check that DFAT can legalise your document and whether you need an apostille or an authentication certificate.
If the document is not an original Australian public document, have an Australian notary public notarise it first.

In person, book an appointment online or hand in the documents at an Australian Passport Office, and pay the fee with a credit or debit card; several documents can be lodged in one appointment.

authorities.scope: Belgian documents signed by a public officer whose signature is on file with the service; some documents need a first certification by a local, regional or federal authority

fees.applies_to: Per document, apostille or legalisation

processing_time.value: At the office, documents of fewer than 4 pages are processed immediately and longer documents are ready the next working day; an e-apostille application made by the issuing authority is normally processed within 48 hours

how_to_steps.text: Check that your document was signed by a public officer whose signature is on file with the service, such as a mayor, an alderman, a notary or a civil servant of a public institution.
Either ask the issuing authority, such as the municipality or the notary, to submit an e-apostille application for you on the eLegalisation website.
In that case payment is made online and a link to the document with the apostille is sent to you by email, with no visit to the office.
Or take the original document, not a scan, to the service at Karmelietenstraat / Rue des Petits Carmes 27 in Brussels between 9 a.m. and noon.
At the office pay by Bancontact or Maestro, Visa or Mastercard, or with proof of payment through B-Post, because cash is not accepted.
Look up or download the apostille on the LegalWeb website with its number and the date it was affixed.

documents_commonly_apostilled.text: Documents signed by a mayor, an alderman or a delegated municipal officer whose signature is on file
Documents signed by a notary
Documents signed by a civil servant of a public institution whose signature is on file with the service
Diplomas, after the education authority of the relevant community has certified them first

special_rules.text: Since 1 May 2018 apostilles can only be affixed electronically.
Documents signed by a notary cannot be handed in at the office; the notary must submit the application on the eLegalisation website.
The service does not legalise copies of passports or identity cards; the issuing authority can instead draw up a certificate repeating the main details, which can then be legalised.
A document in another language must come with a sworn translation, because the service does not translate documents.
Anyone can hand in your document and no identity document is needed.

how_to_steps.text: Work out which competent authority covers your document: Global Affairs Canada, or the province of Alberta, British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec or Saskatchewan.
Prepare a paper document with an original, recognised signature, and notarise it first if the document type needs it.
If any content is in a language other than English or French, add a certified translation.
Submit your request online to Global Affairs Canada.
Send the documents by mail or courier, or drop them off at the distribution centre in Ottawa, with the service request number, a copy of the summary page and a prepaid return envelope or label.
Check the status of the request online; the office can only give status updates for requests it received itself.

special_rules.text: Global Affairs Canada cannot authenticate photocopies, religious documents, foreign documents, documents of unrecognised educational institutions, glued documents or laminated documents.
The document must be on paper, and the apostille is a separate certificate called an allonge that is attached securely to the document.
A document with the old red authentication stamp needs a new request on a clean version if it is to be used in an Apostille Convention country.

A private document can be authenticated after a Canadian notary public has notarised it, and a document notarised in Alberta, Ontario or Saskatchewan goes to that province's authority wherever it was issued.
Apostilles and authentication certificates issued by Global Affairs Canada do not expire.
